memory_update.text: PAR is the highest-priority underfollowed public candidate for the delivery/first-party data rails node because its restaurant software stack directly spans POS, loyalty, digital ordering/delivery, payments, and back office.
Toast remains a direct public restaurant-tech platform for this node, but market cap and attention are higher; treat as a benchmark or mid-cap pure-play rather than obscure supplier.
DoorDash and Domino's define the key strategic tension: aggregator marketplace reach can add demand, while first-party ordering and loyalty preserve customer data and restaurant economics.

Olo would have been one of the cleanest public ordering/data-rail candidates, but it was acquired by Thoma Bravo and delisted in September 2025; monitor private-company disclosures only as ecosystem evidence.
PAR is the strongest underfollowed public mapping for restaurant first-party data rails because it combines POS, loyalty, ordering, and payments exposure at small-cap scale.
Shift4 should remain in the Layer 1 universe as a payments-labeled company with hidden restaurant POS, ordering, loyalty, and analytics exposure through SkyTab.

Toast and DoorDash are high-attention reference anchors: Toast benchmarks integrated restaurant operating-system economics, while DoorDash benchmarks aggregator leverage and marketplace demand access.

Olo was likely the cleanest pure-play public candidate for this node, but it was acquired by Thoma Bravo in September 2025 and should be tracked only as a private-market comp, not as a US-listed candidate.
PAR is a high-priority underfollowed Layer 1B candidate for restaurant first-party data rails because its loyalty, ordering, POS, payments, and operations software directly maps to the node.
NCR Voyix is a hidden-complexity candidate: recent restructuring and legacy NCR labeling may hide restaurant POS, ordering, payments, and loyalty exposure.
Shift4 is a broader payments candidate with restaurant/hospitality exposure; keep it in Layer 1B as an inference pending verification of restaurant mix and SkyTab/POS attach.
The node's chokepoint is not delivery availability alone; the sharper bottleneck is who owns customer access, loyalty identity, order routing, payments data, and direct repeat-order behavior.

Olo would historically have been a direct fit for first-party ordering middleware, but current public-listing status must be checked before inclusion because provided search context indicates a 2025 Thoma Bravo purchase completion.

PAR is a high-relevance underfollowed candidate for the restaurant first-party data rail node because Punchh and Guest360 directly address loyalty, guest identity, ordering, and customer-data activation.

VYX is a low-attention restaurant-tech infrastructure candidate; Aloha POS may be a hidden control layer for online ordering, delivery integration, payments, loyalty, and analytics, but segment-level financial exposure must be verified.

FOUR is a payments-led restaurant data-rail candidate through SkyTab and legacy restaurant POS assets; key diligence is whether restaurant software attach creates durable data/control economics rather than commodity payment processing.

Olo would have been the cleanest public pure-play on restaurant ordering and delivery/guest-engagement middleware, but it was acquired by Thoma Bravo and delisted in September 2025; remaining public exposure is more indirect.

The chokepoint appears to be shifting from delivery availability to control of guest identity, transaction data, loyalty engagement, ordering UX, and POS/payment integration across owned and third-party channels.

node: Delivery channels, first-party ordering, loyalty data, and aggregator partnerships
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Expanded the universe for restaurant customer-access/data rails into a two-lane list. Reference anchors are DoorDash and Domino's because they define the marketplace-vs-first-party ordering tension. The main underfollowed discovery candidate is PAR Technology, a small-cap restaurant software company with POS, loyalty, ordering, payments, and back-office products. Toast is included as a relatively pure public restaurant-tech platform but is less underfollowed and already mid/large-cap. Olo would have been a high-relevance public candidate, but it was acquired by Thoma Bravo and delisted in September 2025, so it is excluded from candidates and retained as a coverage-gap signal. Layer 1B expands the public-company universe around restaurant digital-ordering/data rails. The chokepoint is not simply delivery capacity; it is control of customer identity, order origination, loyalty, payments, POS integration, and aggregator routing. Olo would have been the cleanest pure-play public comp, but it was taken private by Thoma Bravo in 2025, leaving PAR Technology, Shift4, Toast, and DoorDash as the most relevant US-listed public mappings for this pass. The underfollowed lane is strongest in PAR and Shift4 because they sit inside restaurant operating systems rather than consumer-facing delivery apps. Expanded the underfollowed public-company universe around restaurant customer-access and data-ownership rails.
